questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to an English speaking destination and a university with a high academic level.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: We were taken very well care of. Their international office sent us most of the information that we needed to know, and we had an advisor that we could contact in cases where we needed clarification.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Berkeley's International Office held webinars and sent newsletters out.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Dorms, apartments

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Meal plans at the dining halls in dorms

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
It is very expensive. And for the most part, you might have to share a room - it is only possible to get a single room (at least at International House, where I stayed) if you can prove that you are a Master's student. As I was finishing my Bachelor's degree in the fall, I did not have certification of this, but you might if you are a Master's student by the time you are applying. 

But overall, I had an amazing stay at International House and would recommend it if you want to live in a dorm surrounded by people from lots of different cultures and a historic and very beautiful building! Also, the food is great (it is said to be the best dining hall on campus!).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: A lot of courses reserve the seats for students with a specific major or minor (at least for political science and public policy courses) and you have to contact both the professor and faculty advisors in order to get a spot where you tell them what you study at your home university and why you want to take the class and are qualified for it.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You are given access to CalCentral where you can "shop" for courses (add them to your cart). The registration opens on a specific date where you can then enroll in the classes you have added to your cart. It is possible to change your courses, free of charge, until the end of the add&drop period, and after that, it is still possible to add or drop a class, but you have to pay a fee (I think it was around 10 dollars) per added or dropped class.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Course descriptions or contacting your advisor. Googling the course and professors and seeing what other students have said about it.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I ended up getting the classes that I wanted after the end of the add&drop period, where the last seats were opened up.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be aware that you are in charge of creating your own schedule and that it might not be possible to get all the classes you want as some are at the same time or days - and remember that you need to leave space for a lunch break where you have time to go back to your dorm if you have a meal plan.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I felt like the general academic level for undergraduate courses was lower than the bachelor courses at UCPH.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The exchange agreement was an undergraduate agreement. However, it would have been possible to take one graduate course per semester.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The style of teaching was kind of similar. I had two lectures each week for three of my classes and one for my last class. Lectures were two hours long with "Berkeley time" - their version of the academic quarter, but it is only ten minutes - but no break midway (meaning 80 minutes of lecture straight).   Additionally, for two of my classes, I had discussion sections - similar to "holdtimer" at UCPH, where you have a GSI (graduate student instructor) - meaning a PhD or Master's student teaching you like the student instructors at UCPH. These are one hour long, also with Berkeley time (= 50 minutes). 

Attendance was mandatory for most of my classes and a part of the final grade. 

Additionally, you have assignments, quizzes, and midterms for most classes that also count towards the final grade.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
POLSCI 124C: Ethics and Justice in International Affairs
PUBPOL 101: Introduction to Public Policy Analysis
PUBPOL 141: Behavioral Economics for Public Policy
PUBPOL 198: "Directed Group Study" (Impacts of the Showgirl: Taylor Swift)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
POLSCI 124C was really interesting, and the professor was amazing. Would especially recommend if you are into a course that is a mix between International Relations and Political Theory, and you want to write your own research paper instead of taking a sit-in final. However, there are a total of six quizzes which you still have to read the syllabus for.

I also found PUBPOL 101 to be really interesting, but it ended up being kind of similar to the course "Offentlig Politik" on the bachelor of political science - though it focused more on policy analysis specifically, it also covered some of the same theories.

I would also really look into the DeCal courses. These are courses focusing on topics that you would not find on a standard curriculum and therefore a unique chance to focus on something that interests you. Most of them are 1-3 units and therefore also nice to add if you need more units for visa requirements. However, they are not an opportunity for slacking. I had three papers, mandatory attendance for lectures, a midterm debate, and a final presentation in my class (and these were focused on the economic, legal and political aspects rather than just popcultural elements). I do not know if it is like this for every DeCal class or if it is because this specific class counts towards the minor in public policy. It was also 3 units, so it is probably less for DeCals that are only 1 or 2 units.
Be aware that you can only see the DeCals after the beginning of the semester. But I would definitely recommend looking into it and can recommend the class "Impacts of the Showgirl" if it is offered again!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not have to buy books for any of my classes, but we got the readings provided as pdf's. For one of my classes, I had to buy an iClicker for attendance points.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Public transportation in the bay area is free for Berkeley students! You get a travel card from Berkeley that you can use to tap in on busses and the bart (meaning that you can go all the way to San Francisco, the airport, even Palo Alto, completely free!)

Health insurance is mandatory at all UC campuses. You are automatically opted in and assigned to theirs, which is very expensive. I was able to opt out and save a lot of money on health insurance (I think it was more than 10,000 DKK). I found the insurance that I used instead in the Facebook group for UCPH students where another student had recommended it. Be aware of the deadline for opting out - there is a form that you have to fill out, and you need to have already purchased the other insurance in order to fill it out. So make sure that it still lives up to requirements that UC has for health insurance!

Housing is scarce in the Bay Area, including Berkeley, meaning it can be difficult to find something and the options available are very expensive. I really enjoyed the convenience of living on-campus and the environment at International House even though it was expensive. Included in the housing price is a meal plan (it is not possible to buy a room without) - where you get three meals (buffet-style) a day. As mentioned, their dining hall is great, and I would recommend eating all the fresh berries you can to get more value for your money!

Be aware, if you live somewhere off campus and have to cook for yourself, that the cost of living is also very high, and that groceries and restuarants generally seemed a lot more expensive than in Denmark. 
However, I would say that cafés are cheaper than in Copenhagen. Treat yourself to a matcha or an iced latte!!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Different student organizations/clubs, both academic, social, and athletic

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Student tickets for sports games are mostly free, except for some sports. Go see a game against Stanford, the biggest rivals, if you can!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Take the bart to San Francisco and spend the day there, go to RSF (their gym, where membership is free for students), take a hike in the hills, spend the day with your new international friends<3
Also, when it is midterm or finals time, study.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy, people are very forthcoming and nice.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just do it! People are much more open to talking to strangers than in Denmark.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How open people were.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be aware of expenses
2. If you have very high expectations for the academic level, look into taking a graduate course
3. ENJOY!!!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All the people I met!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being so far away for so long!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
